title: Maridebart Cafraglutide (MariTide / AMG 133): Once-Monthly Obesity Drug — Research Dossier
excerpt: Maridebart cafraglutide (MariTide, AMG 133) is Amgen's once-monthly GLP-1R agonist / GIPR antagonist antibody-peptide conjugate. Phase 2 NEJM data shows up to 16% weight loss at 52 weeks with weight still declining at trial end. Phase 3 MARITIME program ongoing. The only once-monthly agent in the obesity pipeline.
content:
Research Disclaimer: Maridebart cafraglutide (AMG 133 / MariTide) is an investigational compound. It is not approved by the FDA or any regulatory agency as of November 2026. Content is for educational and research purposes only. Not medical advice. Consult a qualified healthcare provider before making any health decisions.

What Is Maridebart Cafraglutide?

Maridebart cafraglutide (development codes: AMG 133; trade name candidate: MariTide) is a novel bispecific antibody-peptide conjugate developed by Amgen for the treatment of obesity and overweight. It combines two distinct pharmacological mechanisms into a single molecule and — uniquely among obesity agents in development — enables once-monthly subcutaneous injection.

Unlike the pure synthetic peptides dominating the obesity pipeline (semaglutide, tirzepatide, retatrutide, survodutide), maridebart cafraglutide is a hybrid biologic: a fully human anti-GIPR antibody with two GLP-1 receptor agonist peptide analogs covalently attached to the antibody backbone. The antibody''s natural 21-day half-life extends the peptides'' activity to a full month — three times longer than any weekly obesity drug on the market.

Phase 2 data published in the New England Journal of Medicine (Jastreboff et al., 2025) showed up to 16% body weight reduction at 52 weeks in people with obesity, with weight loss still declining at trial end and no plateau in sight.

Mechanism of Action

Dual Receptor Engagement

Maridebart cafraglutide engages two separate receptor systems through two distinct molecular components:

ComponentTargetEffect
Human anti-GIPR antibodyGIPR (GIP receptor) — antagonismBlocks GIP signaling; reduces fat storage signals; contributes to weight loss
GLP-1 peptide analogs (×2)GLP-1R (GLP-1 receptor) — agonismSuppresses appetite; slows gastric emptying; stimulates insulin secretion; reduces caloric intake

This GIPR-antagonism + GLP-1R-agonism combination is the opposite approach to tirzepatide, which is a GLP-1R agonist plus GIPR agonist. Amgen''s preclinical and Phase 1 data (PMC10896721) showed that GIPR antagonism combined with GLP-1 agonism produced superior weight loss compared to either mechanism alone, and Phase 2 data have supported this hypothesis in humans.

Why Once Monthly?

The monthly dosing frequency arises directly from maridebart cafraglutide''s antibody backbone. Human IgG antibodies are naturally long-lived — their Fc domain binds neonatal Fc receptors (FcRn) that recycle them through the bloodstream, protecting them from degradation. This gives maridebart cafraglutide a 21-day half-life, compared to 7–8 days for semaglutide and tirzepatide. The GLP-1 peptides attached to the antibody remain therapeutically active for the full 30-day inter-dose interval.

Key Research Findings

Phase 1 (Preclinical to Human)

Preclinical and Phase 1 data published in Nature Metabolism (PMC10896721) established the GIPR antagonist + GLP-1 agonist combination''s mechanistic superiority over pure GLP-1 agonism in rodent and non-human primate models, and confirmed tolerability and pharmacokinetics in a first-in-human Phase 1 dose-escalation study.

Phase 2 Trial — New England Journal of Medicine, 2025

Citation: Jastreboff et al., "Once-Monthly Maridebart Cafraglutide for the Treatment of Obesity — A Phase 2 Trial", NEJM, 2025.

Design: Phase 2, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging trial. 592 participants across 11 dose groups in two cohorts.

CohortWeight Change at 52 Weeks (Treatment-Policy)Placebo
Obesity without T2DM (highest doses)–12.3% to –16.2%–2.5%
Obesity with T2DM (highest doses)–8.4% to –12.3%–1.7%
HbA1c change (T2DM cohort)–1.2 to –1.6 pp–0.4 pp

Key observation: Weight loss trajectories were still descending — not plateaued — at 52 weeks in both cohorts, suggesting continued efficacy beyond the trial duration.

Tolerability: Gastrointestinal adverse events (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) were the most common side effects, consistent with GLP-1 class effects. A lower starting dose with gradual escalation reduced incidence. Discontinuation rates were higher in the obesity-without-diabetes cohort — primarily due to GI adverse events — underscoring the importance of dose titration protocols in Phase 3.

Dosing in Research

Note: The following reflects protocols used in clinical trials only. Maridebart cafraglutide is investigational and not commercially available.

  • Route: Subcutaneous injection (once monthly)
  • Doses studied (Phase 2): Multiple dose levels studied across 11 groups; exact Phase 3 doses being optimized
  • Half-life: ~21 days
  • Titration: Phase 2 showed lower starting doses with escalation significantly improved tolerability
  • Duration studied: 52 weeks in Phase 2; Phase 3 registrational trials will determine longer-term outcomes

Frequently Asked Questions

Why can maridebart cafraglutide be injected once a month instead of once a week?

The monthly dosing comes from maridebart cafraglutide''s unique molecular structure: it is an antibody-peptide conjugate, specifically a human anti-GIPR antibody with two GLP-1 agonist peptide analogs attached. The antibody portion has a natural half-life of approximately 21 days — roughly three times longer than weekly peptides like semaglutide or tirzepatide. This extended pharmacokinetics allows the GLP-1 peptide payloads to remain active at therapeutic concentrations for a full month. No other obesity drug approved or in advanced development as of November 2026 offers monthly dosing, representing a meaningful potential compliance and convenience advantage.

What were the actual weight loss results from the NEJM Phase 2 trial?

The Phase 2 trial enrolled 592 adults across 11 dose groups. In the non-diabetic obesity cohort at the highest doses, participants lost approximately 16% body weight by week 52 (treatment-policy estimand) vs. –2.5% placebo. Under the efficacy estimand (excluding post-discontinuation data), values reached approximately 16%–20% at highest doses. Critically, weight loss was still declining — not plateaued — at 52 weeks, suggesting continued efficacy with longer treatment. In the type 2 diabetes cohort, weight loss was approximately 8.4%–12.3% with HbA1c reductions of 1.2–1.6 percentage points vs. –0.4 pp placebo.

Is maridebart cafraglutide a peptide or an antibody?

It is a bispecific antibody-peptide conjugate — an antibody backbone for GIPR blockade and half-life extension, with peptide components providing GLP-1 receptor agonism. It occupies a molecular middle ground between traditional peptides and monoclonal antibodies. We include it because its pharmacological activity is partly driven by the GLP-1 agonist peptides it carries and its development trajectory runs alongside GLP-1 class peptide drugs. This structural note is included so readers understand it is not a simple synthetic peptide.

Research Limitations and Open Questions

  • Phase 3 MARITIME efficacy results not yet available (trials ongoing, completions expected 2027–2028)
  • No FDA or regulatory approval as of November 2026
  • High discontinuation in Phase 2 non-diabetic cohort (GI-related); Phase 3 protocols adjusted for this
  • No published head-to-head comparison vs. weekly obesity drugs (weekly vs. monthly efficacy comparison)
  • Cardiovascular outcomes data from MARITIME-CV not yet available (estimated completion 2028)
  • Long-term safety profile of GIPR antagonism not fully characterized
  • The antibody-peptide conjugate format is novel; regulatory pathway for this molecular class is less established
